query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Directed energy deposition with controlled cooling rates can improve the mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy by reducing compositional segregation, residual stress, and defect formation.
generation.intervention: Directed energy deposition with controlled cooling rates
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain size, reduced porosity, and uniform distribution of elements
generation.mechanism: Controlled solidification and microstructure formation, reduced thermal stresses and hot cracking susceptibility
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, such as increased yield strength and ductility, compared to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi
generation.baseline: Conventional bulk fabrication or mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques
generation.boundary: Limited to cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, additive manufacturing, and thermal processing
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in mechanical properties and the optimal controlled cooling rates are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of mechanical properties between AlCrFeNiSi samples fabricated using directed energy deposition with controlled cooling rates and conventional bulk fabrication or mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi samples fabricated using directed energy deposition with controlled cooling rates are not significantly improved compared to conventional fabrication methods, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Multi-component alloys containing Co, Cr, Ni and other elements have attracted attention recently []. Equiatomic CoCrNi MEAs in particular demonstrate high strength and ductility at low temperatures []. CoCrNi MEAs are typically manufactured by casting and powder metallurgy, yielding a room temperature yield strength of only 360 MPa. Higher mechanical properties require additional processing like rolling, heat treatment and high pressure torsion []. Mechanical alloying (MA) combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS) can also produce CoCrNi MEAs with improved mechanics []. Traditional casting has some shortcomings such as low solidification rate, element segregation and rough casting microstructure, which requires heat treatment to optimize the structure. Compared to traditional casting, LAM can fabricate complex geometries []. LAM enables high cooling rates and temperature gradients, yielding refined solid solution phases and microstructures well-suited for high quality CoCrNi MEAs. Research on CoCrNi MEAs with LAM remains limited. There are many articles on LAM of CoCrNi MEAs. but there are very few articles on HSLAM CoCrNi MEAs. The aim of this study is to investigate the effects of cold rolling and subsequent heat treatment duration on the microstructural evolution and corrosion resistance of high-entropy Cantor alloys. This work specifically focuses on correlating grain refinement, residual stress relaxation, and passive layer formation with electrochemical behavior in order to guide the design of corrosion-resistant HEAs for practical applications. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), such as the Cantor alloy, are emerging materials with unique compositional and structural properties. While conventional alloys such as steel and stainless steel are well studied and widely used in industrial applications [,], the behavior of HEAs under various processing conditions remains unclear due to limited data on their performance in different manufacturing and service environments [,]. In particular, the electrochemical behavior of the high-entropy Cantor alloy after cold rolling has not yet been fully investigated []. In addition, its microstructural evolution and corrosion resistance following cold working and subsequent heat treatment remain underexplored. These approaches enable more accurate prediction of phase formation and mechanical properties, guiding alloy design and reducing experimental trial and error. Fabrication of engineering parts from high-entropy alloys (HEA) using additive manufacturing (AM) has been increasingly studied in the past five years. Initial studies focused on powder bed fusion of CoCrFeNi, a prototype single-phase high entropy alloy with face-centered-cubic (fcc) structure, from pre-alloyed powders, and observed increased strength and ductility compared to cast alloys. Later, the Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni system was predominantly studied, either as equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi or as AlxCoCrFeNi with 0.1 < x < 1. Other work demonstrated AM of CoCrFeMnNi by selective laser melting, Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.5Mo0.1 by directed energy deposition, ZrTiVCrFeNi by electron beam melting, and polymer-AlCoCrFeNi composites by coating 260 nm thick 3D printed polymer nanolattices with 14–126 nm thick HEA shells. It is typically observed that AM processing through the liquid state, followed by solidification at high cooling rates, refines the grain size, leads to finer precipitates in two-phase alloys, and produces a highly textured microstructure; however, it may require high preheating temperatures to attenuate cracking, and it leads to inter-dendritic segregation of elements and microstructural g

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) belong to a new class of materials that are chemically concentrated in less-explored phase spaces. Since their initial discovery,, HEAs have attracted tremendous interest for their remarkable structural diversity and unique electrical, magnetic, and mechanical properties,, including high strength and great ductility. While HEAs were initially modeled as random solid solutions, recent works have focused on the possibility of chemical short-range ordering (CSRO) and its unusual effects on microstructural, mechanical, and electronic properties. Particular attention has been given to the medium-entropy alloy (MEA) CrCoNi. This alloy, which belongs to a family of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys, has demonstrated superior mechanical properties, irradiation resistance,, and quantum criticality at low temperatures. Especially, the close proximity of ferromagnetic (Co and Ni) and antiferromagnetic (Cr) interactions can lead to magnetic frustration, and the concept of magnetic-driven CSRO has inspired multiple experimental and theoretical works.
